Pele Yoetz 185:14: All prayers and supplications should be said with a truly broken heart and proper intent, for humility is a very great foundation for purifying a person and for prayers being accepted; therefore one should not raise his voice loudly, but rather all his prayers should be in a hushed voice of supplication and a voice of weeping. Now one who understands the Holy Tongue should take to heart and make his own ears hear what he is saying, dwelling deeply on every word in its full breadth, and with the greatness and loftiness of the exalted and uplifted King before his eyes, and his own great lowliness and poverty and the weight of his sins, let him greatly humble his heart and be embittered. “Let the poor man speak in weeping and supplication, perhaps there is hope.” It is fitting for those who fear God to write in the margins of their books various means of arousal for every prayer and every supplication, to serve as a reminder before their eyes to awaken their hearts, and let him write down everything found written in the books plus whatever he adds from his own knowledge. And let him also write precise readings, for many errors have crept into the printed books. And year after year let him keep adding, to give merit to himself and to whoever the book reaches, that they may copy from it. And let him also write the meaning of certain words and matters that are not easy to understand at first glance, so that the reader may run through them easily. And one who cannot manage to understand the meaning of the words in the Holy Tongue — it would be well for him to go to a wise man who will teach him, so that at least he will have in mind what the subjects of the prayers are.
Pele Yoetz 185:15: In any case, it is the duty of every person to have the fear of God upon his face always, all day, and to feel truly as though standing in judgment before an exalted and uplifted King, awesome and terrible, and to constantly think holy and pure thoughts, in a manner that his eye weeps bitterly while his heart is glad, anxious yet trusting, and his heart should not turn to idleness even for a moment, nor should his mouth cease from study all day and most of the night; yet he should manage his affairs with judgment, so that he does not stay up learning all night lest the labor of the day become too heavy for him, and his gain come out as his loss — except that when he sees the fatigue of the year's accumulated weariness falling upon him on the night of Yom Kippur, he should not force himself, but rather lie down at once and rest. And he should rise before daylight if he can, and increase his study, and especially his prayers and supplications for the sake of Heaven's concerns, and all his aim, desire, request and petition should be that God help him, for the sake of the honor of His Name, to do His will as He wills, to give delight before His Throne of Glory, for we have no measure better than this, and this is the whole of man — and on whom do we have to rely if not our Father in Heaven, for were it not that He helps us, we could not do any good thing at all, for we have become very poor and lack all good. And if they said (Rosh Hashanah 18a) that prayer during the Ten Days of Repentance is accepted even for an individual, as it is written (Psalms 69:14), “As for me, my prayer is to You, O Lord, at a time of favor,” and it is written (Isaiah 49:8), “In a time of favor I have answered you,” and it is written (ibid. 55:6), “Seek the Lord while He may be found” — how much more so on Yom Kippur, for it is the day of favor above all days, and the gates of favor are open.
Pele Yoetz 185:16: Therefore he should not turn to idleness even for a moment. And it is written in the books that when a person engages in Torah and supplications on Yom Kippur for even one hour, it is worth more than a whole day on other days; therefore one should be very careful with this day, for it is passing. And one who is negligent in it, failing to do all that is in his power to do, loses much good. And how greatly one must stand on guard during these days, and especially on Yom Kippur, not to stumble into any hint of transgression, for the punishment of the sinner is heavy in these days and at this time, when there is no fear of God before his eyes, and perhaps the scale of his sins will grow heavy at the time of weighing, and he will come out guilty in his judgment, and thereby become liable for his life.
Pele Yoetz 185:17: And especially one must be careful not to transgress the five afflictions, which are the commandment of the day; and just as one is careful about eating and drinking, so he should be careful about washing, not washing his face at all, nor washing his hands beyond the joints of the fingers, and he should not wear leather sandals at all. Although there are those who permit this in the streets among gentiles, this is not the practice of the pious, especially nowadays. And regarding the affliction of marital relations, we have heard a warning not to touch one's wife as though she were a niddah. And a person should consider that on this day we say “Blessed be the Name of His glorious kingdom forever and ever” aloud, because we resemble the ministering angels; and if we are not careful and diligent to stand on guard in holiness and purity, in awe and fear and trembling, to the utmost of our ability, what comparison could there be between us and the ministering angels — would not the ministering angels mock us? Therefore let every person clothe himself in dread and wrap himself in trembling, and let him do all the good that is in his power in thought, speech and deed, and let him resolve in his heart, with a peaceful heart and a willing soul, to abandon the wicked man's way and walk in the way of the good, keeping the paths of the righteous, in order to raise up the Divine Presence from the dust, and to arouse love and give delight to our Creator, for this should be the aim of all our prayers and commandments, our study and our repentance. These are some of the paths of righteousness fitting to follow on these mighty days and on Yom Kippur, and then one will merit to be inscribed in the book of good life among the upright and pure. (And your eyes will see what I have written under the entry Rosh Hashanah, and under the entry Sheliach Tzibbur, and under the entry Selichot, and under the entry Teshuvah.) Let the wise man hear and add learning.
Pele Yoetz 186:1: Kofeh (Subduing) — The whole purpose of man's creation on earth is only so that he may subdue his inclination and enjoy the fruit of his labor in the World to Come, and merit to behold the pleasantness of the Lord and to visit His sanctuary, for “one who has not eaten does not rush to look at” [the reward] (Yerushalmi Orlah 1:3). And were it not for the evil inclination, man would have no true reward, for he would be like the ministering angels, and there would have been no need for his coming into the world; but the Holy One, blessed be He, formed man for His own honor, that the honor of Heaven be increased, and when a person subdues his inclination and does the will of his Maker, this is a great delight to our Creator, when human beings who are mighty in strength do His bidding. And according to the toil, exertion and the strength of the evil inclination overcome, so does he increase the delight to our Creator, and the reward is according to the pain.
Pele Yoetz 186:2: And it is written in Sefer Chasidim that for one commandment where a person's inclination provokes and overpowers him to make him transgress the will of his Maker, and he subdues his inclination, he receives reward equal to a hundred commandments where his inclination does not overpower him. And this is the meaning of the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Berachot 34b): “In the place where penitents stand, even the completely righteous cannot stand.” For since the righteous are righteous from the outset, they do not have the incitement of the evil inclination as much as penitents do, whose habituation to sin makes it hard for them to separate from it, like tearing the nail from the flesh; thus, when they overcome their inclination like a man of war and subdue their inclination, they give great delight to our Creator and their reward is greater. And this is how the earlier scholars explained the saying of our sages, of blessed memory (Berachot 8a): “Greater is one who enjoys the fruit of his labor than one who fears Heaven [by nature].” Meaning, greater is one who enjoys the fruit of his labor — having labored much to conquer his inclination — than one who fears Heaven by nature, for one who enjoys the fruit of his own labor has it better for the World to Come. Thus it is fitting to rejoice over the evil inclination that is within us, for through it we give delight to our Creator, and through it we merit the great reward given to the righteous.
Pele Yoetz 186:3: And behold, it is written in Sefer Chasidim that for every transgression that comes to a person's hand and his inclination overpowers him, he should consider that if they were to decree that he change his religion, he would certainly give his life to death for the sake of the honor of His blessed Name; and subduing one's inclination is even harder and more bitter than death; so let him subdue his inclination for the sake of his Maker. And behold, our eyes see that almost all of Israel are presumed fit to give their lives for the sanctification of the Name, yet there is not even one who fully subdues his inclination and becomes a righteous man on earth who does good and never sins at all. The reason is that one who gives his life to death does not have as much incitement from the inclination, either because the sin of changing religion is very grave in everyone's eyes — unlike other transgressions, which the evil inclination makes seem small in people's eyes, as they explained on the verse (Genesis 6:5), “And every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil” — or because he thinks that death is but a moment, and in any case a person must eventually die, and by giving his life for the sanctification of the Name he is immediately saved from his inclination and is destined for life in the World to Come; whereas this is not so regarding subduing his inclination against other transgressions, which is harder for him, since his inclination will always pursue him, and Satan stands at his right hand to accuse him.
Pele Yoetz 186:4: But in truth, the masters of ethics have already written (Chovot HaLevavot, Gate of Repentance, ch. 27) that one should not regard the smallness of the transgression, but rather the greatness of the Master who commanded concerning it, and whoever transgresses the command of the King, whether small or great, is called a rebel against the kingdom. And they further wrote that one who follows the counsel of his inclination, even transgressing a light sin, is considered as one who worships idolatry; for just as an idol-worshipper abandons the Lord and accepts upon himself some star or constellation as a master and patron, so too does this person accept his inclination as a master and patron to be his judge. And there are several ways to make the pile larger, that any small transgression should be counted like the thick ropes of a wagon. Moreover, since his inclination overpowers him to commit a transgression, it incites him more than it incites him against giving his life to death; therefore the reward of one who subdues his inclination is greater than that of one who gives his life to death, for the reward is according to the pain, and so does he give delight to his Maker and so is his reward given. And the Lord in His mercy will never forsake His pious ones who struggle with their inclination; only the beginnings are hard, and once they become a little accustomed to walking in the way of the good, then the feet of His pious ones are guarded, and their hearts become empty within them, and doing good becomes sweet and pleasant to them, and their soul no longer desires to do evil, and He credits them with great reward as though they had always subdued their inclination, for everything follows the beginnings, they all ascend together.
Pele Yoetz 186:5: And as he increases doing good and conducting himself with piety, in the end he reaches a level where no sin comes about through him, and no mishap results from his hand, as our sages, of blessed memory, said (Chullin 7a): “Even regarding the animals of the righteous, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not bring about mishap through them” — how much more so the righteous themselves. For once he has reached this level, they proclaim about him in the heavens, “Be careful with so-and-so the Rabbi,” in such a way that the wicked man watches for the righteous, but the Lord will not abandon him into his hand (Psalms 37:32).
Pele Yoetz 186:6: And the reason the Holy One, blessed be He, does not let the evil inclination provoke the righteous is that since He knows the way of the righteous, and it becomes known to all the heavenly host how strong and mighty they are, that they are mighty in strength to subdue their inclination, then there is no need to trouble them, and it is only right that they receive their reward in full, for what advantage has the owner except the sight of his eyes; and even though everything is revealed and exposed before Him, the Holy One, blessed be He, wanted all the heavenly host to know that the Lord is righteous and His judgment is righteous, that He gives to a man according to his ways. And as they explained in the holy Zohar on the verse (Genesis 22:1), “And God tested (nissah) Abraham” — that the term “nissah” does not apply to the Holy One, blessed be He, in the sense of a trial, but rather in the sense of raising a banner (nes). And so He created the evil inclination, so that through it, before the eyes of all, it becomes known that the righteousness of the Lord and His judgments were done, and that they are sustained by [His] mighty arm. And since permission was given to the Destroyer to entice and incite, he also entices the wicked, and the fools passed by and were punished. It follows that the Holy One, blessed be He, did not create the evil inclination in order to punish the wicked, God forbid, for God does not desire wickedness or vengeance against His creatures, but rather in order to give a good reward to the righteous, who subdue their inclination and give delight to their Maker.
Pele Yoetz 186:7: And it is true that according to this, inquiry finds room to pause and investigate: why did the Holy One, blessed be He, create the wicked, especially those who have no share in the World to Come, for whom it would certainly have been better had they not been created — since He foresees and beholds to the end of all generations, why did He create them in this world? Was it in order to take vengeance upon them by having them anger Him and cause blemish and damage above? Heaven forbid such a thing of a merciful and gracious King, the Master of mercy, whose mercies are upon all His works. This very question was already asked in the holy Zohar, Parashat Shelach Lecha, and the answer given there was that the ways of the Holy One, blessed be He, are hidden and concealed, supernal mysteries which He keeps sealed and hidden — we have no right to ask, see there. These are wondrous things beyond the perfect Knower; we can only believe with complete faith that the Rock, His work is perfect, His work is pure and upright, and injustice does not dwell in His tent, God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 186:8: And included in the commandment of subduing is being firm in words and in every manner of coercion, in whatever way is within one's power, toward every person, so that he walk in the way of the good and keep the paths of the righteous (Proverbs 2:20). And one should withhold his hand from doing any evil, in the manner of what they said (Bava Batra 8b), “They coerce for the sake of charity.” This is the commandment of rebuke and the commandment of protest for one who has the power to protest. And behold, Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, commanded Joshua and said to him, “Take a rod and strike upon their heads” (Sanhedrin 8b). And they said (Ketubot 103b), “He threw bile among the students.” And there are several matters where, according to the law of the Gemara, there is an obligation to strike with whips and rebuke sharply in order to set the people straight; but I say that just as, regarding the healing of the body, the generations and the natures and the remedies have changed — remedies that were beneficial in ancient times have no benefit now — so too regarding the healing of the soul the generations have changed, and in these generations, when insolence increases, people do not accept authority, and the crooked become ever more crooked.
Pele Yoetz 186:9: Thus, one who wishes to set the people straight, and especially those lacking knowledge, should coerce them only with good, gentle and sweet words. This is fitting, and perhaps the listener will listen and accept his words, for a soft tongue breaks a bone (Proverbs 25:15), and by this he releases enmity from himself, and is saved from causing his fellow to go out to bad ways through him, thereby adding transgression to sin, and thus transgressing “you shall not place a stumbling block before the blind” (Leviticus 19:14); and he is also saved from strife and quarrel and many other evils that are prepared to come from harshness. But one who conducts himself with a soft tongue is beloved above and cherished below; the spirit of humankind is at ease with him, and the spirit of the Omnipresent is at ease with him.
Pele Yoetz 186:10: And behold, one who deals with someone who lacks understanding must have double the understanding, to conduct himself with him according to his traits and views, with pleasant speech, in such a way that his eyes will see and his heart will understand which is the straight way, and thus be healed; but one whom the Lord has graced with proper understanding endures harshness and rebukes and does not depart from the proper line even if it happened that he was treated improperly. And I heard a story that happened in our generation in a certain city: there was a wealthy man there, very God-fearing, whose hand was powerful, who used to sit at the gate of the lord of the land. And once the local rabbi, the moreh tzedek [halachic authority] of that city, was found in anger and sent to speak harshly against him, almost over nothing, while the wealthy man was dining with the nobles and dignitaries of the city; and he immediately turned his face toward the nobles who were with him and said to them, ‘What do you think — that this message the rabbi, the moreh tzedek, sent against me is a disgrace to me, God forbid? This is nothing but great honor, that he honors me before you by showing that he regards me as a good man, one who fears God, on which basis he relied to speak to me thus, even though he knows I have power and could harm him, God forbid — yet he is not afraid of me, since he knows me and recognizes me. This is a great honor to me.’ Happy is the people who has such complete and proper understanding, and happy is he who dwells with him in the same neighborhood.
Pele Yoetz 187:1: Kohen (Priest) — Heaven has sanctified the kohanim with extra sanctity and extra commandments, and it befits them, more than others, to keep the charge of holiness and to conduct themselves with even greater piety, in the manner of what is written (Malachi 2:7), “For the lips of a priest should guard knowledge, and Torah should be sought from his mouth.” And especially regarding their own commandments they must be extra careful, for little remains to them nowadays, such as the commandment to bless Israel, which contains three positive commandments, and the one who blesses is himself blessed by the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is written (Numbers 6:27), “And I will bless them.” And how greatly have those kohanim erred who go outside the synagogue in order not to bless Israel, thereby losing much good! (“Who would grant me to be a kohen, that I might lift up my hands every day.”) Likewise they must be careful regarding impurity from the dead and from women forbidden to the priesthood, and they should conduct themselves with dignity, not giving their daughter to an unlearned Israelite, nor should an unlearned Israelite risk taking a kohen's daughter, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (Pesachim 49b) that a match between a kohen's daughter and an [unlearned] Israelite does not turn out well: either she becomes a widow or divorced, or has no offspring, or she buries him or he buries her, or it brings him to poverty. And for one who does not know this, “the Lord preserves the simple” (Psalms 116:6); but one who knows the saying of our sages, of blessed memory, should guard his soul and not transgress the words of the Sages. And one must show honor to kohanim, as our sages, of blessed memory, expounded (Mo'ed Katan 28b) on the verse (Leviticus 21:8), “And you shall sanctify him.” And it is forbidden to make use of a kohen [for personal service] unless he is hired and comes for his wage.
Pele Yoetz 188:1: Kafuy Tovah (Ingratitude) — It is written (Proverbs 17:13), “Whoever repays evil for good, evil will not depart from his house.” And it is incumbent upon a person who has received any kindness whatsoever from his fellow that it be engraved in his heart forever, all his days, not to repay him with any evil, but rather to repay the doer of the kindness with whatever is in his power, even if that person also did him some harm — he should forget the harm and not forget the kindness, for a person must have some of his Maker's own quality in him. And it is written (Isaiah 49:15), “Even these may forget” — referring to the deed of the [golden] calf — “but I will not forget you” — referring to the giving of the Torah. Go and learn from Moses our teacher, who did not strike the Nile or the dust, because he had received benefit from them (Tanchuma, Va'era 14). And likewise our sages, of blessed memory, said (Bamidbar Rabbah 22:4) that Moses did not take vengeance upon Midian himself, because he had been raised among them. And our sages, of blessed memory, said in Shemot Rabbah (4:2): whoever opens a door for his fellow is more obligated to honor him than to honor his own father and mother. You find this with Elijah, who did not revive his own ancestors as he revived the son of the woman of Zarephath, and Elisha did not revive his own ancestors as he revived the son of the Shunammite woman, but rather he gave his life for the sake of his host. And if one is so obligated to show gratitude to his fellow for a piece of bread, how much more so if he received much benefit from him, and how much more so, doubled and redoubled, if he received from him a benefit to his soul, such as being taught wisdom or being guided on a good path and kept from an evil path, which is a good so great that there is none greater — how much more must his obligation grow to recognize the good done to him and treat him with honor; and if he does not treat him with the honor due him, there is no ingratitude greater than this. And on that day, let him reason a fortiori regarding himself: how much more is a person obligated to his Creator, who abundantly does good without measure to the House of Israel — so great, without measure, is our obligation.
Pele Yoetz 189:1: Kevi'ah (Burn) — When it happens to a man that he is slightly burned by fire or something derived from fire, let him surely remember what the sinning soul passes through in chastisement for sin, for this fire is only one-sixtieth of Gehinnom, and there they burn the sinning soul seven times every day — four at night and three by day — and they become ash and then return and stand upon their standing again. “Passing through the Valley of Baca, they make it a place of springs” (Psalms 84:7); our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Eruvin 19a) that this means they weep and shed rivers and streams of tears. And how harsh are the judgments of Gehinnom, to a degree that none of us, while in the body, is able to picture, and every judgment of Gehinnom is as nothing compared to other, even harsher judgments done to the wicked. And it is already a common saying among people that when they are slightly burned they groan a little and say, “Woe to us, the province of Gehinnom,” but what benefit is there when they do not withdraw their hands from doing all manner of evil?
Pele Yoetz 189:2: But this is the teaching of the person who believes in the Torah and in the words of our sages, of blessed memory, who explained the judgment of the wicked (Eduyot end of ch. 2), and that the Holy One, blessed be He, does not forgo His due (Bava Kamma 50a), but rather gives to a man according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds for every transgression — let him have pity on his own soul, spirit and neshamah, and not destroy himself knowingly, and let him reckon the reward of a transgression against its loss; for it is true that He increases good measure, and there is much good for one who performs even a single commandment, but the Holy One, blessed be He, does not take bribes, and even if one is completely righteous, but transgressed one sin in his youth or old age and did not repent as is proper, when he departs from the world, they say to him with honor, “Enter Gehinnom first, in order to pay your debts and suffer punishment according to the sin, and afterward you shall go to tranquil rest.” Thus, whatever is in one's power to do — repentance and good deeds, and to withdraw one's hand from every evil thing — while he is alive, let him do so and continue to add to it, before the days of evil come.
Pele Yoetz 189:3: And I said this as a hint regarding the custom of the world: that when one is slightly burned by the touch of a burning coal, he touches his earlobe, and they say this is a remedy for the burn to pass. And I said it is a hint, that since through the burn he is reminded of Gehinnom, he touches his earlobe to remember that limbs are burned there first (Ketubot 5b). And there is also a hint here, as if to say: you cause me to be burned in Gehinnom; the name that I heard I do not uphold, I did not listen to the voice of my teacher — for one who hears and fulfills is indeed complete, as it is written (Isaiah 55:3), “Listen, and your soul shall live.” And incidentally I will tell the generation that there is a remedy for every kind of burn: let the burned person, or another on his behalf, recite the Priestly Blessing three times with intention, and it will help — this is tried and tested.
Pele Yoetz 190:1: Kelev (Dog) — One who hears dogs crying and howling, especially if they are howling at a person at night in the darkness, jumping upon him and biting him, his heart is greatly afraid. Let him then surely remember what the sinning soul passes through when it is handed over to destructive agents and angels of harm resembling dogs and other evil beasts. Even David the king, peace be upon him, prayed about this and said (Psalms 22:21), “Deliver my soul from the sword, my only one from the power of the dog.” And while his eyes are still open, let him have pity on the soul, spirit and neshamah, that it not be handed over to fierce dogs. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Bava Kamma 83a) that one who raises dogs is like one who raises pigs, for he stands under a curse and withholds kindness from his household. And many common people are not careful and raise dogs, and it is fitting to inform them of the severity involved. And if one wishes to raise a dog to guard against thieves, let it be tied with a chain, so that it does not lock the door before everyone who comes in [in need], and thus he will avoid punishment. And our sages, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 155b), “None is poorer than a dog, and it is proper conduct to throw it a bone.” And from this a person should learn to have mercy on every living being.
Pele Yoetz 191:1: Keni'ah (Submission) — Submission is a matter of great importance in the eyes of God and man, for we find that Ahab was saved from the evil occurring in his days through submission, as it is written (I Kings 21:29), “Have you seen that Ahab has humbled himself,” etc. And according to what the Kabbalists have written, the essential acceptance of prayer depends on humility. And a story once happened that a group of the righteous prayed with wondrous intentions, and it was revealed to them from Heaven that the prayer they had said was indeed wondrous, but because they lacked humility they were liable to be punished, were it not for one among them who had humility, and through his merit they were all saved. Great are the humble of spirit before the Holy One, blessed be He, and their prayer does not return empty. Thus, one should be firm in strengthening himself to have a broken and contrite heart, especially when saying any prayer, any supplication — let him humble himself greatly, like a small worm upon the earth, and as nothing, mere vanity. And this is easy for us, for with a little reflection we recognize our own smallness and the weight of our sins, and what are we and what is our life compared to the greatness of our Master. However much we humble ourselves, we do not fulfill our obligation, and part of our lowliness is that we do not recognize even one part in a thousand of our deficiency and lowliness compared to the greatness of our Master, and this suffices for one who has a heart, only that he place these words upon his heart at all times, and especially when he speaks with his Maker — this should be his thought, and from this he will find his redemption.
Pele Yoetz 191:2: And also toward other people, submission is a very sharp remedy: for if a man sins against his fellow and does him many wrongs, if he submits to him and says, “Indeed I have sinned against you and acted crookedly, forgive me,” his fellow will immediately be won over and reconciled to him, even if his fellow was angry at him and his heart was burning like fire — this one comes and pours water on the fire and extinguishes it. Therefore this is the straight path: even if one has claims and answers regarding what he did, if he sees that his fellow is angry, and he is a lover of peace and pursuer of peace, let him not seek claims and answers, but immediately say, “True, I erred and sinned, please forgive me, I ask.” Likewise, one whose fellow, or even a gentile, strikes him or curses and reviles him, and he submits before him and accepts everything as though the judgment were with him, and is silent — then the one who struck him will be shamed, and his wrath will subside, and the enemy will become a friend. And this is what the commentator explained on “let him give his cheek to the one who strikes him” (Lamentations 3:30) — meaning, that he bows before him and says, “Strike,” then the one who struck will be sated with disgrace, and it will be a remedy for him [the one struck]. Examine this trait closely and you will find it a beautiful trait, like fine flour sifted through thirteen sieves.
Pele Yoetz 192:1: Kesef (Money) — It is written (Proverbs 10:20), “The tongue of the righteous is choice silver.” And it is written (Ecclesiastes 7:12), “In the shadow of wisdom, in the shadow of money.” Observe and see that it likens money to the tongue, and money to wisdom — there is a hint here, that just as they said (Arachin 15b), “Death and life are in the hand of the tongue — whoever wants life, [let him seek it] with his tongue; whoever wants death, [he finds it] with his tongue,” and likewise they said (Kiddushin 30b) that the Torah is likened to a perfect medicine — whoever wants, it is a medicine of life; whoever wants, it is a medicine of death — so too we shall say regarding money: whoever wants, [finds] life through money; whoever wants, [finds] death through money. For most transgressions are drawn from a person's greed for money, such as robbery, theft, fraud, exploitation, false oaths, false swearing, lies, dishonesty in measures, encroachment on another's boundary, strife, envy, hatred, rivalry, forbidden foods, desecration of Shabbat and festivals — most transgressions a person commits are for the sake of monetary gain, and the sin of desecrating God's Name rides upon them. Likewise, one to whom his money is precious neglects many commandments, prayers and blessings, and Torah study more than all of them; and when he does perform them, they are invalid due to his haste and stinginess, his heart not being with him, for his mind is turned toward gain wherever he turns, and he averts his eye from charity, and “what he should do, he does not do,” and many other evils, such that there is wealth kept by its owner to his own harm, through which he inherits Gehinnom and descends to the pit of destruction.
Pele Yoetz 192:2: And indeed they said (Eruvin 65b), “A person is recognized by his pocket,” for it is true that the enemy, the inclination for wealth, has grown mighty, especially in this generation, a generation of money, where a person is more obsessed with money than with all transgressions and all pleasures, and a person's money is dearer to him than even his body, and even more than his soul. But this is the teaching of man in this world: that he should be a mighty man who conquers his inclination (Avot 4:1), and open his eyes and see that “silver gathers souls, and gold causes souls to pine away,” and understand the truth of the matter, that it is better for a person to die of hunger than to be wicked before the Omnipresent and anger his Creator, God forbid.
Pele Yoetz 192:3: And let a person be firm in strengthening himself to be mighty in conquering his inclination, and let money be considered as nothing in his eyes compared to doing the will of the Creator. Thus he will treat silver like stones in order to do the will of his Father in Heaven. And let him believe with complete faith, fixed in his heart like nails that will not be moved, that his sustenance is allotted to him from Heaven; even if the heavens were to rise and the depths sink, they could not add or subtract from him even a single penny — except for expenditures on commandments and good deeds, which are not fixed, for if he adds, they add to him. Thus there is one who acquires his world through his wealth, by increasing charity, increasing commandments and good deeds, and acquiring a good name for himself, acquiring for himself words of Torah, acquiring for himself life in the World to Come. And they have already fixed the mnemonic “a matter of Torah is acquired with money” (Eruvin 81b, Bava Metzia 46b, 47b), for all matters of Torah and every good thing requires money, and money answers everything. Whoever is wise will heed these things and not be lulled to sleep. The end of the matter, all having been heard: fear God and keep His commandments, for this is the whole of man (Ecclesiastes 12:13).
Pele Yoetz 193:1: Kinnuy (Nickname) — Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Bava Metzia 58b) that one who gives his fellow a demeaning nickname has no share in the World to Come. And they said (ibid.) that this applies even if he merely repeats that name, for which he already has become accustomed. And it is forbidden even to call one's fellow by his [demeaning] nickname. And due to our sins, the affliction has spread and it has become as though permitted to call one's fellows by a demeaning name or by their nickname, until they forget their real names — and this is one of the matters that Scripture weighs as equally severe as the gravest of sins, for our sages, of blessed memory, said (ibid.), and we believe in their holy words and live by their teaching, that he has no share in the World to Come. Thus, whoever fears the Lord and fears for his own soul should guard his mouth and tongue from this and the like, and not destroy himself knowingly. And if one wishes to mention someone's name and does not know his proper name, or wishes to mention the man to others who do not know him by his proper name, he should be careful to say, “that man whom people call so-and-so,” for even though by this the man is cleared of the sin, it would be better still to rebuke plainly the people walking in darkness and inform them of the prohibition and its severity, until they return to calling him by his proper name, for the merit of the many depends on it.
Pele Yoetz 193:2: And we have already heard a warning to be especially careful in mentioning the names of rabbis, not to call them by their nicknames, as some are accustomed to say “HaRav Karo,” “HaRav Alshech,” “HaRav Algazi,” and the like; rather one should say “Moreinu HaRav Yosef Karo,” “Moreinu HaRav Moshe Alshech,” for if there is a prohibition regarding other people, how much more so regarding our holy sages.
Pele Yoetz 193:3: And there are things that it is a commandment to rename with a demeaning term, such as idolatry (see Sanhedrin 63b), which it is forbidden to mention by the name the gentiles call it, and likewise the festival days of the gentiles, which one must rename with a demeaning name. And many are not careful, not understanding what the name the gentiles call it means — whether it is in praise of the idol — or out of lack of knowledge, and one must be careful. And especially when speaking with gentiles, if one cannot rename it with a demeaning name, he must be careful to steer the conversation so as not to need to mention the name of the idolatry or its festival days, which are called by the name of their idolatry, so as not to transgress what the Torah said (Exodus 23:13), “And the name of other gods you shall not mention.” Likewise one should be careful to speak in a language of honor and clean language, and to rename shameful matters with euphemisms; for instance, regarding relieving oneself, one should say “he went to attend to his needs,” whether major or minor, and likewise when mentioning a place of filth, he should call it “beit hakisei” (the seat) or “beit hakavod” (the house of honor). And likewise when speaking of matters of marital relations, he should speak in clean language, in the Holy Tongue. Let the wise man hear and add learning, for a person is recognized by his words — the base person speaks base things, while a man of honor speaks only of honor.
Pele Yoetz 194:1: Kallah Beit Aviha (The Bride in Her Father's House) — There are places where, while a bride is betrothed, she has a close acquaintance with her groom, and they have set days when they see each other face to face, such as on Chanukah and Purim and the festivals and the like, and they sit side by side and talk together and laugh together, and other evil customs of this kind found in the cities of Italy and the cities of Ashkenaz and some cities of Turkey. And this evil custom has already been cried out against in the books, for just as it is impossible for fire in tow not to flare up, so it is impossible for the groom to escape an unintentional emission, which is a criminal transgression, so much so that our sages, of blessed memory, said (Niddah 13b) that one who deliberately causes himself an emission should be under a ban. And from this he comes to spilling seed in vain, which is a grave sin, considered like killing a soul and as though bringing a flood upon the world, as is known, the astonishing severity of this prohibition. And even if he escapes the actual transgression, he does not escape improper thoughts; one cannot say “and He will hold him innocent.” Behold, then, an obligation rests upon whoever has the power to correct and to protest for the sake of the honor of His Name, that he roar like a lion and go out to meet the weapon to abolish this evil custom. And such mixing of men and women singing and dancing together, where Satan dances among them and the fire of the evil inclination burns within them, they cannot escape either transgression or improper thoughts. Let this matter be forgotten and let there be no such thing in Israel.
Pele Yoetz 194:2: And how good and pleasant is the custom of some cities of Turkey, where the groom does not see the bride's face until the moment of the chuppah. Let the righteous man hold to this way. And if he cannot correct it for all the people of the city, let him correct it for his own sons and for those who join him and submit to his authority, for truly our sages, of blessed memory, said (Kallah ch. 1) that a bride [married] without a blessing is forbidden to her husband like a niddah. And because of this sin and the like, firstborn young sons die of the sins of youth, and a woman miscarries. Thus one who loves his sons will guard them from every sin and transgression, and especially from this grave sin, for it is a matter of taking a life. And it is best not to arrange the marriage of one's children except close to the time of marriage, so that they not be preoccupied and infatuated over the bride, and no mishap occur, and instead relief and salvation, joy and gladness stand for them.
Pele Yoetz 195:1: Ketivah (Writing) — Writing, how great is its benefit! It is a commandment upon the father to teach his son the craft of writing, for without it a person cannot lift his hand either in mundane matters or in matters of Heaven. And one who does not set his heart to it and does not know the craft of writing properly, in the Holy Tongue and in the vernacular, shame and disgrace will cover him. And it is part of perfection to strive to also teach square script writing. And how good and pleasant it would be if he could himself fulfill the commandment of writing a Torah scroll for himself. And for one who has the standing of a Torah scholar, it is incumbent upon him to accustom and train himself to write in the Holy Tongue with good eloquence, each matter expressed in its proper way, for from a person's words one recognizes whether he is a Torah scholar; and if he speaks with a stammering tongue and a cut-off language full of mistakes, he will become a laughingstock and mockery, and he brings deficiencies upon himself. Therefore the complete man, who desires to acquire perfection, should also open his eyes to this. And the benefits of writing are too many to count; happy is he who holds fast to them. And I shall record in writing some of them; let the wise man hear and add learning.
Pele Yoetz 195:2: Behold, one whom the Lord has graced with knowledge and placed his portion among those who sit in the study hall — how good it would be for him to record in writing everything the Lord has graced him to originate, whether a small or a great novel insight, and let him not be lax, for they have already said (Sefer Chasidim, sec. 530) that a person will in the future be held accountable for not having written in a book everything revealed to him from Heaven in Torah novellae. And they further said (ibid.) that one who writes Torah novellae, it is accounted to him as though he had offered sacrifices, and through the writing the matter becomes revealed, and it is as though he had taught it among tens of thousands of the myriads of Israel, as the Rambam wrote. And a time will come when his lips will move in the grave, and he will sate his soul with delights. And if the Lord has graced him with an eloquent tongue to know how to rebuke with the rod of his mouth, and he writes a book of ethical rebuke and summaries of needed laws and the like, it will surely happen at some time that his words will bear fruit even for one in a thousand, and then happy is he and happy his portion, for if he had come into the world for this alone, it would suffice.
Pele Yoetz 195:3: And likewise, through writing he can record a memorandum of things he needs, whether for remembrance or to recite aloud, such as prayers and supplications and the like. Therefore it is good for a man to also teach his daughter the craft of writing, so that she may learn to bless and pray and study books in the vernacular and learn to fear the Lord. And also through writing, records of accounts are kept — who owes and who is owed — and all the affairs of his shop, so that he not falter. And also through writing, letters are sent to distant places, and he accomplishes his affairs and his hands suffice for him; and especially when he writes letters of greeting to his household and to his relatives far from him, it is counted to him as a great commandment, to revive the hearts of the downtrodden, in such a way that even one whose Torah is his profession need not worry about wasting time for such a matter — provided he is careful that his tongue not be a sharpened arrow speaking slander in his writing, and that he not become a sower of discord, God forbid. What more shall I say — and for well-known matters no proof is needed — that the craft of writing is greatly needed and is a thing equally valuable for every soul. Thus, let a man be firm in strengthening himself to teach his son, or himself, the craft of writing in all its conditions and details, for its benefits are many.
Pele Yoetz 196:1: Kilyot (Stinginess) — Stinginess is a very evil trait, for it makes one begrudge his poor brother, and he averts his eyes from charity, which is like worshipping idolatry (Bava Batra 10a), and “what he should do, he does not do,” and his eye is evil even regarding his own [belongings], to the point that whoever eats of his bread eats the bread of an evil eye, and he increases strife within his household over the minutiae of poverty, and increases prohibited matters and wrongs between man and his fellow, and many other evils. In sum, the miser's vessels are evil — evil toward Heaven and evil toward humanity. He will not be ashamed in this world, and he will not be shamed in the World to Come [i.e., there is no remedy]. And the person who is God-fearing and tenderhearted should be firm in strengthening himself and persist in studying books of ethics, and wage war with strategies, and trust in the Lord and do good, and the Lord will not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 196:2: Indeed, frugality is necessary, that one not squander and waste and make excessive expenditures where unnecessary, for the Torah has regard for the money of Israel, and even the value of a single perutah should be very significant in his eyes, that he not allow it to be wasted, for so we find with Jacob, peace be upon him, who endangered himself for small jugs, because the righteous hold their money dear, since they do not stretch out their hands in robbery (Chullin 91a). And even for the wealthy of the people, who do much good, this is not thereby a permission for them to squander and waste and transgress “do not destroy,” for they have not yet made all the poor wealthy, and they are destined to give account and reckoning for how they spent the money entrusted to them; and especially Torah scholars and their wives and all members of their households — it is incumbent upon them to be very precise in their expenditures, not to spend except on what is essential and cannot be done without, and their whole aim should be to minimize expenditure as much as possible, and not to be particular about lacking finery in clothing and jewelry and fine foods, wines and oils and the like, but rather to make do with little, so that the Torah scholar not need to be troubled and reduce his work — the work of Heaven, God forbid — and their portion in life suffices for them, a world that is entirely good. And if the wife of the Torah scholar acts thus and watches over the ways of her household as is proper, how good is her portion, for she takes the first share in the Torah, which is more precious than pearls; and also all members of the household and all who assist the Torah scholar will take their share.
Pele Yoetz 196:3: Complete and finished is half the book. With God's help, He gives beauty in place of ashes.
Pele Yoetz 197:1: Kelalut (Generalities) — Part 2: Kelilat Yofi (Perfection of Beauty) — One learns from generalities. Behold, I have now undertaken to complete what I resolved to record in generalities, briefly and forcefully, a reminder of the sin about which people are not careful, and its severity, and upright conduct which a person should follow and live by them. Let me gather sayings from the mouths of books, as far as my feeble hand can reach. Whoever desires life, let these things be a remembrance before his eyes. Day by day let him utter them. Let the wise man hear and add learning; let him remember and not forget. “If you have chosen life” and to escape destruction, “turn from evil and do good.”
Pele Yoetz 197:2: 1. First in the reckoning of sins: slander, which is equal to idolatry, illicit relations, and bloodshed (Arachin 15b). And slander is speaking ill of one's fellow about something not publicly known, even if speaking the truth. Whoever desires life, guard your tongue from evil, and let him make himself like a mute, not to speak of his fellow whether good or bad.
Pele Yoetz 197:3: 2. Pride and irascibility are a criminal sin, like denying the fundamental [of faith] and like worshipping idolatry (Sotah 4b, 5a), and one who has it will not rise at the resurrection of the dead, and he will live a life of suffering, and all who see him will disdain him. And one who does the opposite is filled with merit, and all this on account of his humility and self-effacement, remembering that he is lower than all the lowest of creatures, since he angers his Creator, and “every haughty heart is an abomination to the Lord” (Proverbs 16:5). And our sages, of blessed memory, said (ibid. 5a): whoever has pride is placed under a ban.
Pele Yoetz 197:4: 3. Anger is as severe as idolatry, and it tears its owner's soul in his fury, and all his Torah and commandments go to the Sitra Achra [the Other Side], and there is no remedy for him ever, until he takes upon himself not to become angry; and if he transgresses, let him fine himself with some affliction, or with money for charity, and he will be healed.
